common_name: Blue Belle Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Blue Belle is one of the original University of Saskatchewan haskap releases and needs a compatible pollinizer cultivar with overlapping bloom time planted nearby.

directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Belle is self-infertile. Blue Belle was one of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Bird, and Blue Moon) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that brought large-fruited modern haskaps into wide North American cultivation. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening two to three weeks ahead of standard blueberries in most climates. Like other haskaps, Blue Belle is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving winter temperatures to -40F with flowers tolerating brief dips to about -8F, but it is not well suited to hot, humid summers and performs best in cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the shrub productive.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Haskap Cultivar Release Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

common_name: Blue Moon Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Blue Moon is one of the original University of Saskatchewan haskap releases and needs a compatible pollinizer cultivar with overlapping bloom time planted nearby.

directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Moon is self-infertile. Blue Moon was part of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Belle, and Blue Bird) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that established large-fruited modern haskaps in North American gardens and orchards. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often described as a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening well ahead of standard blueberries and giving cold-climate gardeners one of the first fresh berry harvests of the season. Like other haskaps, Blue Moon is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F with flowers surviving brief dips to about -8F, but it performs poorly in hot, humid summers and is best suited to cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first three to four years to removing dead or crossing branches, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes.
